$comment: WHAT GOES INSIDE THE INSTALLER BESIDES THE VIEWER.
ToolsEnabled is one half of a product. The other half is the
capability layer it talks to: the action bridge it discovers on
127.0.0.1, the tool registry behind that, and the MCP server that
exposes the same registry to agent clients. Before this manifest the
installer shipped `dist/**` and `shell/**` only, so a customer
installed a viewer with nothing behind it and every write action
answered BRIDGE_UNREACHABLE.
The payload is derived, not listed. `entrypoints` are the two programs
the product actually starts; pack-capability-layer.mjs walks their
require() graph and stages exactly the reachable files. That closure
originally contained only project JavaScript. The ordinary require graph
still rejects npm dependencies; separately pinned provider runtimes declare
their exact quota-only dependency bytes. Electron's own binary runs
the layer under ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE.
`dataFiles` is the part a require() walk cannot see: JSON the layer
reads at runtime through readFileSync on a computed path. Each entry
below was found by starting the staged payload in a directory with no
checkout and reading what it failed on -- not by guessing.
`neutralDefaults` names the data files whose real contents describe
the BUILDER (their machines, their seats, their accounts) and would be
both a privacy leak and factually wrong on a customer's machine. The
packer stages capability-defaults/<path> in their place; see those
files for what a fresh installation truthfully declares.
$comment_hostModules: MODULES THE SHELL REQUIRES OUT OF THE PAYLOAD, rather than programs the
payload starts.
`entrypoints` answers 'what does this payload RUN'. That question missed
an entire directory: src/lib/setup/ is reachable from tools/mcsetup.js --
a command-line program -- and from nothing the bridge or the MCP server
requires. So the shipped payload contained no setup code at all, and the
permission-level question that docs/design/INSTALLER-EXPERIENCE.md 2.1
calls the product's first impression could only ever be asked from a
developer's checkout.
These are walked into the closure exactly like an entrypoint, so their own
require() graph ships too and the same fail-closed rules apply. They are
listed separately, and recorded separately in PAYLOAD.json, because they
are NOT startable: shell/setup-record.cjs require()s them in the Electron
main process. Calling them entrypoints would make bridgeEntrypoint
ambiguous and tell the next reader the payload starts three programs.
The last eight entries were added 2026-09-07. The shell also loads payload
modules by composing the path at the call site --
require(path.join(root, 'src', 'lib', 'accessibility.js')) -- with no
literal module string anywhere, so they were named in no list here and
shipped only because something else in the closure happened to require
them. They were measured PRESENT in the staged payload at the time, so
this declares what was already true rather than adding files; the point is
that it stops being true by accident. The loader is fail-soft, so an
omission produces no error, only a product that quietly does less.
$comment_licenseTrustAnchor: config/license-trust.json IS THE ODD ONE OUT IN dataFiles, AND DELIBERATELY SO.
Every other entry is JSON that staged code reads today. This one is the PUBLIC
half of the vendor licence signing key, and the code that reads it --
src/lib/providers/license.js -- is classified `paid` in
config/payload-boundary.json and is NOT in this payload. So it ships with no
reader, which normally would be a reason to leave it out.
It is staged anyway because of what its ABSENCE did. Licence verification is
pinned to this anchor and fails closed without one; the anchor file did not
exist anywhere in the source tree, so every verify threw
LICENSE_TRUST_ANCHOR_MISSING and no paid licence could be activated by anyone,
for weeks, with no gate red. The failure was invisible precisely because the
missing thing was a file nobody had listed. Listing it here means the day the
paid layer enters this payload its anchor is already beside it, instead of
reproducing that outage on a customer's machine.
IT IS SAFE TO SHIP. A public key lets you CHECK a signature and never FORGE
one -- that is the whole point of asymmetric signing. The private half lives
only in the vendor's DPAPI vault under vault/secrets.json, which
assertNoSecretMaterial() below refuses to stage by prefix AND by basename.
tools/test/license-trust-anchor-payload.test.mjs asserts both halves of that
against the STAGED BYTES: the public key present, no private key material
anywhere in the payload.
$comment_capabilityIndex: config/capability-index.json IS BUILT, NOT WRITTEN, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS LISTED HERE.
It is the searchable index of the tool catalogue that src/lib/capability-recall/
reads to answer 'which tools might fit what this person just typed'. The engine
builds it from its OWN tool registry (node tools/build-capability-index.js) and
its gate refuses to write one where any tool is unreachable, so the file is
derived from the same catalogue the payload ships and goes stale the moment a
tool is added, removed or re-described.
It is read through a computed path -- rootPath('config', 'capability-index.json')
-- so the require() walk cannot see it, which is the exact condition this list
exists for. It sat under data/ in the lane it was built in; nothing under data/
reaches a customer, so an index built there would have shipped to nobody and
answered nothing, which is the trap context/ and tools/grepsaver-orient.js
It is ~650 KB, the largest single entry in this list. That is the whole
vocabulary for 271 tools; it is parsed once per process and shared frozen, so a
fleet of agents costs what one costs.
$comment_diagnosticQualificationSupport: tests/helpers/diagnostic-memory-fs.js supplies the in-memory filesystem for
the mandatory diagnostic facade and panel checks against this exact packed
Engine. It imports only Node assert/path, never real filesystem operations.
Shipping this one helper keeps those checks independent of a source checkout.
$comment_helperPrograms: PROGRAMS THE LAYER RUNS THAT ARE NOT JAVASCRIPT, and the reason this
category had to exist rather than being folded into `dataFiles`.
The require() walk sees JavaScript. It cannot see a PowerShell script
reached through rootPath('tools', 'secrets.ps1') and handed to
powershell.exe, and it never could -- that path is a string, computed at
runtime, in a spawn argument. So the single most load-bearing file in the
product shipped in no installer at all: tools/secrets.ps1 IS the secret
vault. Without it src/lib/runtime.js vaultScript() throws 'Secret vault is
not installed', which means no credential can be read AND -- measured, not
reasoned about -- src/lib/audit.js cannot fetch its Ed25519 signing key, so
every tool call on a customer's machine ran with the canonical audit ledger
silently refusing every write. The privacy policy promises that ledger in
writing. The tool call still returned success, which is why no gate caught
it for as long as the gate only asked whether a window appeared.
These are copied verbatim, exactly like `dataFiles`, and the packer could
have carried them there. It does not, for two reasons. First, `dataFiles`
documents itself as JSON-read-through-a-computed-path, and a list whose
name and comment stop describing its contents is how a manifest quietly
starts lying. Second, and the reason that matters: a program and a data
file have different SHIPPING RULES. tools/secrets.ps1 is a program and must
ship; vault/secrets.json is that program's storage and must never ship.
Naming them apart is what lets assertNoSecretMaterial() in the packer state
that rule mechanically instead of leaving it to whoever edits this file
next. The packer refuses any entry here that is not one of the executable
extensions, and refuses any staged path under vault/ or state/ outright.
Found the way the `dataFiles` comment prescribes: by starting the staged
payload in a directory with no checkout, with LOCALAPPDATA, USERPROFILE and
CODEX_HOME redirected to empty directories, and reading what it failed on.
TWO HELPERS LEFT THIS LIST, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. owner-identity-profile.ps1
and private-identity-evidence.ps1 stage and OCR the builder's own passport and
legal-identity records. They were declared here because the JavaScript that
spawns them was staged, and a payload carrying the caller without the script is
a feature that is present and broken -- worse than one that is absent. Both
JavaScript modules have since left the require() closure (their tool
definitions moved to src/lib/tool-packs/), so the scripts leave with them and
nothing in the payload is left pointing at a missing program. Removing a helper
before its caller would have inverted that, which is why they moved together.
windows-job-wrapper.ps1 is the native Windows Job Object seam started by
src/lib/windows-job-control.js. The JavaScript require walk carries its caller
but cannot see the computed PowerShell spawn path; declaring it here keeps the
installed timeout/cancellation tree boundary identical to the tested source tree.
secrets-manager.ps1 IS THE SECOND VAULT PROGRAM, AND IT WAS MISSING FOR THE
SAME REASON THE FIRST ONE WAS. src/lib/secret-store/powershell.js resolves it
as programOrStatePath(ROOT, ['tools', 'secrets-manager.ps1']) -- a computed
path in a spawn argument, invisible to the require() walk, exactly like
secrets.ps1 above. Measured in the staged payload at app c8deb5e4: secrets.ps1
present, secrets-manager.ps1 absent. Its absence is not a missing diagnostic.
It is the whole secret LIFECYCLE half of the vault: run() fails closed with
SECRET_MANAGER_NOT_INSTALLED, so inventory(), history() and mutate() all throw,
which means system.credential_remove -- the product's ONE generic way for an
owner to delete a stored credential -- cannot work on an installed build, and a
key the owner has revoked at the provider stays on his disk with no route to
remove it. secrets.ps1's own 'del' verb is reachable but is deliberately not a
generic export (see the clearDeviceCredential comment in src/lib/runtime.js), so
there is no second door. Pinned by tools/test/vault-manager-staged.test.mjs.
$comment_spawnedPrograms: JAVASCRIPT PROGRAMS THE PAYLOAD ITSELF STARTS -- the third answer to 'what
runs', after `entrypoints` (what the SHELL starts) and `hostModules` (what
the SHELL require()s).
src/job-runner.js is spawned by src/lib/providers/scheduler.js to execute a
scheduled action; tools/lane-run.js by src/lib/agent-wake.js; the local-coder
sidecar worker by src/lib/providers/overnight-advisory-runtime.js; the
local-node lane runner by src/lib/mission-bridge/actions.js for every
local-model dispatch (its absence from this list is why a customer with a
working Ollama got a child that died on MODULE_NOT_FOUND -- measured
2026-08-19 against the sealed build; the engine now also refuses that
dispatch honestly with BRIDGE_LOCAL_RUNNER_MISSING). Every one
is reached through a computed path, so the walk cannot see them, and every
one has its own require() graph, so copying them verbatim like a helper
program would ship an entrypoint whose first require() throws.
They are therefore walked as closure ROOTS, on the same fail-closed terms as
an entrypoint, and recorded separately in PAYLOAD.json for the same reason
`hostModules` is: the shell must never be told the product starts six
programs when it starts two.
tools/relay-shell.js (added 2026-08-21) is the machine leg of the relay: the
program that lets a signed-in browser reach THIS computer over the sealed
tunnel. It was classified open in the engine's source boundary from the
start and was never in the payload, because nothing the payload ran reached
it -- so no installed copy could answer a relay, whatever supervised it. It
is a root here for the same reason the others are: reached by the shell
through a computed path, with its own require() graph (the whole
online-fra-* family: device identity and claim, the e2e session, the relay
client, the local bridge). The shell spawns it only once a machine is
enrolled, and never for writes while the owner's web-drive switch is off.
tools/online-fra-claim-cli.js (added 2026-08-21) is what makes that
enrolment possible in the first place: the three verbs -- open, poll,
status -- that join this computer to a person's account. It was written to
be the one implementation every surface drives, and then shipped to none of
them, so the only way to connect a machine was to run it by hand out of a
checkout the customer does not have. shell/device-claim.cjs spawns it here
the same way the relay leg is spawned, and reads the vault answer that
decides whether the relay leg starts at all. Its whole require() graph is
already staged (src/lib/online-fra-device-claim.js and src/lib/runtime.js
arrive with tools/relay-shell.js), so declaring it a root stages the CLI
itself and nothing else.
tools/resolve-node.js is the JavaScript authority invoked by the shipped
tools/lib/resolve-node.ps1 helper. PowerShell dependencies are not visible
to the JavaScript require walker, so this explicit closure root is what keeps
the installed coordinator registrar from failing before it can qualify Node.
src/lib/vault-host/worker.js is started through a computed Worker path by
vault-host-client.js. Its require graph and the tools/vault-host.ps1 helper
must ship together; otherwise every persistent vault request waits for a
worker that is absent before falling back to a one-shot process. The host
dot-sources the existing secrets.ps1 under its unchanged action allowlist.
$comment_dynamicRequires: The require() calls whose argument is computed at runtime, so a static
walk can see that a dependency exists but not what it is. Each is
declared here with the exact expression it was found as; the packer
stages `resolvesTo` and walks it like any other dependency, and REFUSES
any computed require that is not declared. That refusal is the point:
the day someone adds a new dynamic require, the build stops here rather
than shipping a payload that throws MODULE_NOT_FOUND on a customer's
machine, where nobody is reading the console.

dynamicRequires.$comment: coordinator-duty-host reaches exactly these two product modules through optionalModule(ctx, name, relativePath). Both call-site paths are fixed literals; declaring both makes the installed closure complete while the runtime dependency-injection seam remains testable.

Declared so the packer's computed-require guard is satisfied, and resolved to NOTHING on purpose: capability-features.js carries the commercial tier table, and the free payload must not ship a byte of it (tools/test/free-payload-licensing.test.mjs). The caller degrades through its own catch with the stated reason capability-features-unavailable.

audit-admission-worker runs on a worker thread and must not import the controller layer that owns the tool-meter ledger: the package checker counts that edge as KERNEL_IMPORTS_UP debt. So the caller passes its module specifier with the request and the worker loads only what it was handed, fenced to its own directory (METER_LEDGER_PATH_INVALID otherwise). The specifier is a fixed literal at the single call site: controller-tool-meter.js declares METER_LEDGER_MODULE = './controller-meter-ledger' and passes it to recordToolMeterBatch. The target is already staged by the static walk, so declaring it adds no bytes; it makes an existing edge explicit and keeps the dependency-injection seam testable.

pointer records that same commit, and the source worktree is detached there so

That source begins at clean engine commit b44d0e9 and overlays only the reviewed
source-derived runtime bytes plus the neutral organisation parity example. Its
RELEASE-SOURCE.md records the construction. Repacking selects 299 source files
and six app-owned neutral defaults: 305 payload files, 7504865 bytes, payload
SHA-256 6cd2d97ece46e2fc8f22d5208ca687a2faa2edca8139965fd794c1f43a17b80c,
with a clean owner-data result and zero file/hash differences from capability/.
The live engine worktree contains unrelated unfinished clusters and is not a
release input. The loose engine-payload directory is retained only as reviewed
byte evidence; it is not a Git checkout and therefore cannot satisfy the build's
two-repository provenance gate. Do not repoint either record without reviewing
the complete derived closure and flipping the pointer and this record together.
THE LOCKSTEP THIS ENTRY EXISTS FOR, restated because it was nearly broken again:
src/lib/multi-account/rotation.js is named in hostModules above, classified open
in config/payload-boundary.json, and present at the pinned ref. All three or none.
A manifest naming a module the pinned source does not carry is what made the app
suite red while every layer beneath the button already worked.
THE ACCOUNT LIST IS USER DATA AND IS NOT IN THIS PAYLOAD. The registry lives at
<state root>/accounts.json, written by the accounts page on the machine that owns
it. The builder's own config/accounts.json names his personal accounts, is
classified excluded in the engine boundary, and is named in no manifest list here
-- deliberately, because shipping it would ship an identity, and shipping an empty
one would be a file whose only content is the absence of content. Absence already
means "no rotation", truthfully and for free.

$comment_providerRuntimes: Quota-only public SDK closures are built from their committed lockfiles and pinned per-file manifests. Generated files are hash checked before and during staging; extra files and symlinks are refused. This does not allow arbitrary npm imports in the ordinary capability closure.
